title: Caring for Widows and Church Leaders
overview: Paul gives Timothy practical instructions for treating people in the church like family, supporting widows who have no one else, and handling church leaders fairly.

parts.label: Treat everyone like family (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Timothy was a fairly young leader, so he is told to correct older men gently, as he would his own father, and to treat others as brothers, mothers and sisters. With younger women he must keep things completely pure, so that closeness never turns into anything improper.

parts.label: Widows truly in need (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: Widows often had no income, so the church gave real support, which is part of what "recognition" or "honor" means here, to those left with no one at all. If a widow had children or grandchildren, they were to look after her first, and anyone who neglects their own family is called worse than an unbeliever, because even people without faith usually care for their relatives.

parts.label: The list of widows (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: There was an official list for widows over sixty who had been "the wife of one man" (read by some as faithful to her husband, by others as married only once) and who were known for kindness, such as raising children, welcoming travelers and washing guests' feet. Scholars are unsure whether this was simply a list for aid or a recognized group of older women who served the church in return.

parts.label: Younger widows (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: The writer worries that younger widows on the list may later want to remarry and so break their "first pledge", which may mean a promise to serve the church or a vow not to remarry (scholars are unsure), or may drift into gossip that gives outsiders reasons to mock the church. So he advises them to remarry and run homes, a view shaped by its era that many modern readers find hard, and asks believing women with widows in their family to support them so church funds reach those with no one.

parts.label: Fair treatment of elders (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Church leaders who lead well deserve "double honor", which most readers take to mean both respect and pay, backed by an old law about letting a working ox eat and a saying also found on Jesus' lips. Accusations against them need two or three witnesses, as in Israel's ancient law, and those who keep doing wrong must be corrected openly, with no favorites.

parts.label: Personal advice to Timothy (vv. 22-25)
parts.note: "Laying on of hands" was how new leaders were appointed, so Timothy should not rush it, since some people's faults and good qualities only show up over time. In between, Paul tells him to drink some wine for his stomach, likely because water was often unsafe and Timothy was frequently ill.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the rules about widows describe an early recognized ministry role for women and on how far these culture-shaped instructions should guide churches today.
think: Who do you feel responsible to care for, and where does that sense of obligation come from?
